stem: A high severity alert fires on Friday evening, a ticket is created automatically, and nobody looks at it until Monday. Which automation capability was missing?

options.text: Escalation: automatic routing onward when a ticket is not acknowledged within a defined time
options.why: Ticket creation worked; the gap is what happens when nobody picks it up. Escalation exists to remove the dependency on one person being available.

options.text: Ticket creation
options.why: The stem says the ticket was created. The failure is downstream of that.

options.text: Alert tuning
options.why: Tuning addresses alerts that should not have fired. This one was high severity and genuine.

options.text: Continuous integration testing
options.why: That runs checks on code changes and has nothing to do with alert handling.

stem: A team adds dependency checks, static analysis and secret scanning to run on every pull request, failing the build on a critical finding. Which automation use case is this, and what is its primary benefit?

options.text: Continuous integration and testing, catching flaws while they are cheapest to fix and before they reach production
options.why: Shifting the check to commit time means the author fixes it with the context fresh, rather than it becoming a production finding someone else inherits months later.

options.text: Guard rails, preventing insecure resources from being created
options.why: Guard rails constrain what can be provisioned at deployment or runtime. These checks act on the code before anything is deployed.

options.text: Ticket creation, since failures generate work items
options.why: A side effect at most. The capability described is the testing gate.

options.text: Escalation, since the build failure notifies the team
options.why: Escalation routes onward when nobody responds. A failing build is immediate feedback to the author.

stem: An orchestration platform enriches an alert with asset owner details, opens a ticket, and disables the affected account, all without a human relaying information between systems. What makes this possible?

options.text: Integrations and APIs exposed by each system
options.why: APIs are the plumbing orchestration runs on. Without a programmatic interface on each system there is nothing to orchestrate and a person ends up copying values between consoles.

options.text: Guard rails configured on the cloud platform
options.why: Guard rails constrain what may be created. They do not connect tools to each other.

options.text: Continuous integration pipelines
options.why: CI concerns building and testing software, not connecting operational tooling.

options.text: Standard infrastructure configurations
options.why: Those make deployments consistent. They do not let one system call another.

stem: A team automates a fragile manual process with a large set of custom scripts written by one engineer who then leaves. Which named risks of automation does this illustrate?

options.text: Complexity, ongoing supportability and technical debt: the automation now needs maintaining by people who did not write it
options.why: The objectives list these as costs of automation precisely because undocumented bespoke tooling becomes a second system nobody understands, often less reliable than the process it replaced.

options.text: Only cost, since scripts are cheap to write
options.why: The writing is cheap and the owning is not. Cost here means total cost over the lifetime.

options.text: A single point of failure in the network
options.why: Single point of failure does appear in this objective, and it refers to the automation itself becoming one, not to network topology.

options.text: None: automation always reduces risk
options.why: The objective explicitly lists its costs, which is why it asks about benefits and risks together.

stem: An organisation routes all provisioning, access changes and incident response actions through one orchestration platform. What risk does this introduce?

options.text: The platform becomes a single point of failure: its outage stops provisioning and response simultaneously, and its compromise grants all of those capabilities at once
options.why: Concentrating capability concentrates both the outage and the prize. The objectives name single point of failure as a cost of automation for exactly this reason.

options.text: Reaction time will increase
options.why: Orchestration improves reaction time, which is one of its listed benefits.

options.text: Employee retention will fall
options.why: Retention is listed as a benefit: removing repetitive work tends to keep people, not drive them away.

options.text: Baselines can no longer be enforced
options.why: Enforcing baselines is one of the things such a platform does well.

stem: The objectives list employee retention as a benefit of automation. What is the reasoning?

options.text: Automating repetitive low-value work lets skilled staff spend time on work that uses their judgement, which is what keeps them
options.why: Burnout in security operations is driven heavily by volume of repetitive triage. Removing it is both a workforce multiplier and a retention measure.

options.text: Automation reduces headcount, so fewer people need retaining
options.why: The objectives frame automation as a workforce multiplier, making existing staff more effective rather than replacing them.

options.text: Automated systems do not require training
options.why: They require different and often deeper skills to build and maintain.

options.text: Retention improves because automation reduces salary costs
options.why: Reducing pay is not a retention mechanism.

stem: A team automates ticket creation from a detection source that currently produces a 70% false positive rate. What is the predictable outcome?

options.text: A backlog of mostly worthless tickets that trains everyone to ignore the queue, so the real findings are buried faster than before
options.why: Automation scales whatever you point it at. Pointed at noise, it industrialises the noise, which is why tuning has to precede this kind of automation.

options.text: Improved response times, since every alert now has an owner
options.why: Ownership of noise is not improvement. Mean time to respond on genuine findings usually gets worse.

options.text: The false positive rate will fall as tickets are closed
options.why: Closing tickets does not change the detection logic producing them.

options.text: Escalation will resolve the problem automatically
options.why: Escalation would route the same noise to more senior people faster.

stem: Which security outcome most directly improves when account disablement is automated from the HR leaver feed rather than handled by ticket?

options.text: Reaction time: access is revoked within minutes of the HR record changing rather than whenever someone processes the request
options.why: The window between departure and revocation is where dormant-account risk lives. Automation closes it to the latency of the feed.

options.text: Efficiency, because fewer tickets are raised overall
options.why: True and secondary. The security outcome is the shortened window.

options.text: Baseline enforcement across endpoints
options.why: A different use case, concerning configuration rather than identity.

options.text: Reduced technical debt
options.why: Building and owning the integration tends to add maintenance burden, not remove it.

stem: Which TWO are listed by the objectives as costs or risks of automation rather than benefits? (Choose two.)

options.text: Technical debt and ongoing supportability
options.why: Automation is software, and software has to be maintained by whoever inherits it.

options.text: The automation platform becoming a single point of failure
options.why: Concentrating capability concentrates both outage impact and the value of compromising it.

options.text: Acting as a workforce multiplier
options.why: A listed benefit: the same team covers more ground.

options.text: Improved reaction time
options.why: A listed benefit, and often the main reason for doing it.

options.text: Enforcing baselines consistently
options.why: A use case and a benefit, not a cost.

stem: An audit finds three leavers still had active accounts weeks after their last day. Which automation use case addresses this?

options.text: User provisioning and de-provisioning driven by the HR system
options.why: Tying account lifecycle to the authoritative HR record removes the manual step that was missed, in both directions.

options.text: Guard rails on resource creation
options.why: Guard rails block a non-compliant action as it is attempted. Nobody attempted anything here; a step simply never happened.

options.text: Automated ticket creation for the service desk
options.why: Closer, and it still depends on a human picking the ticket up. The access is what should be removed automatically.

options.text: Continuous integration and testing
options.why: CI runs checks on code changes. It has no view of employment status.

stem: Engineers keep creating cloud storage that is readable by anyone on the internet. Which automation concept prevents the action rather than reporting it afterwards?

options.text: Guard rails
options.why: A guard rail refuses the non-compliant action at the moment it is attempted, so the exposure never exists.

options.text: Automated reporting to a dashboard
options.why: That tells you after the bucket is already public. The stem asks for prevention.

options.text: Security group membership automation
options.why: Security groups decide who belongs to what. They do not constrain how a resource is configured.

options.text: Ticket creation and escalation
options.why: Raises the work item once the problem exists. Still after the fact.

stem: Which is a genuine drawback of heavily automating security operations?

options.text: The orchestration platform becomes a single point of failure
options.why: When provisioning, access and response all route through one system, its outage or compromise is an outage or compromise of all of them.

options.text: Response times increase
options.why: Reaction time is one of automation's clearest benefits. It acts in seconds.

options.text: Baselines become harder to enforce
options.why: Enforcing baselines consistently is exactly what automation is good at.

options.text: Staff retention gets worse
options.why: The objectives list employee retention as a benefit: removing repetitive work keeps people.

stem: A team automates host builds from a single template. A misconfiguration is later found in that template. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Automation multiplies whatever it is given, so one bad baseline reaches every host
options.why: The property that makes automation valuable, perfect consistency at scale, is the same property that scales a mistake.

options.text: Automation is unsuitable for host builds
options.why: Manual builds drift and are worse. The lesson is to review the template, not to stop automating.

options.text: Templates should be replaced by manual configuration
options.why: That trades one consistent error for many inconsistent ones and loses enforceable baselines.

options.text: The misconfiguration proves the automation failed
options.why: The automation did exactly what it was told. The failure is upstream, in what it was told.

stem: A small security team automates triage of low-severity alerts. Which benefit does the exam call this?

options.text: A workforce multiplier
options.why: The same number of people cover more ground. The objectives name this explicitly alongside efficiency and reaction time.

options.text: Risk transference
options.why: Transference moves financial impact to a third party, such as insurance. Nothing moved outside the organisation.

options.text: A compensating control
options.why: A compensating control substitutes for one you cannot implement. Automation here improves a control you already have.

options.text: Defence in depth
options.why: Layering independent controls is a different idea. This is throughput.

stem: Developers sometimes launch cloud servers without disk encryption. Which automation prevents this before it happens?

options.text: A guard rail that rejects or auto-corrects non-compliant resource requests
options.why: Guard rails enforce policy at provisioning time, so the insecure option cannot be created.

options.text: A ticket opened for each unencrypted server found later
options.why: Ticketing records the issue after the fact. It does not prevent it.

options.text: A scheduled report listing unencrypted servers
options.why: A report is detective and depends on someone acting on it.

options.text: A script that runs on one engineer's laptop
options.why: A single-person script is a single point of failure and does not cover other users.

stem: A SIEM alert should create a ticket, add the asset owner, and page on-call if untouched for 15 minutes, with no manual steps. Which capability makes the tools work together this way?

options.text: APIs and integrations between the tools
options.why: APIs let one system trigger, query and update another, which orchestration relies on.

options.text: A larger analyst team
options.why: The aim is to remove manual steps, not add people.

options.text: Longer log retention
options.why: Retention affects how long data is stored, not how tools hand work to each other.

options.text: A more complex password policy
options.why: Password rules do not connect systems.

stem: A security team automates dozens of workflows with undocumented scripts. The author leaves, and a vendor update breaks several of them. Which two automation drawbacks does this show?

options.text: Technical debt and poor ongoing supportability
options.why: Undocumented custom automation becomes hard to maintain once its author leaves.

options.text: Faster reaction time and a workforce multiplier
options.why: Those are benefits, not what failed here.

options.text: Lower cost and employee retention
options.why: Those are benefits. The scenario shows maintenance cost rising.

options.text: Standard configurations and scaling securely
options.why: These are uses of automation, not drawbacks.

stem: A security officer wants new hires to receive the right access on day one and leavers to lose it the moment employment ends. Which approach delivers both?

options.text: Automate user provisioning and deprovisioning from the HR system
options.why: Tying account changes to HR events removes delay and human error in both directions.

options.text: A quarterly manual access review
options.why: Reviews are periodic and manual. Leavers keep access until the next review.

options.text: An approval ticket for each change
options.why: Ticketing records work but does not remove the delay.

options.text: A guard rail on cloud storage
options.why: Guard rails constrain resources, not account lifecycle.
